newsitem.title: USA: Energy Dept finalizes plutonium disposal plan.
newsitem.headline: Energy Dept finalizes plutonium disposal plan.

text.p: The Energy Department Tuesday gave the final go-ahead to a controversial two-track program to scrap 50 tons of plutonium left from the nuclear weapons program.
Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said she signed the policy to immobilize some of the plutonium in glass or ceramic, and mix the rest into fuel to be used in nuclear power plants.

While the department announced this plan last month, O'Leary said it had added measures to ensure that using plutonium in civilian reactors does not compromise efforts to halt the spread of nuclear weapons ingredients.
Most nuclear control advocates want the department to immobilize the plutonium and bury it to prevent its commercial use and keep it from ever being used in weapons.
In a telephone news conference, O'Leary said the department would immobilize at least eight tons of plutonium because it needs too much purification to be used in fuel.
She also said the department would immobilize the plutonium at its Savannah River site in South Carolina, and would not have to build another facility.
In the plan to use plutonium in civilian reactors, the department said there would be no reprocessing and extraction of residual plutonium from the spent fuel.

It also said the mix-oxide or MOX fuel for reactors would be fabricated in a "domestic government-owned facility at a secure DOE (Department of Energy) site," ruling out potential European facilities.
The facility would be licensed and used only for weapons plutonium disposition. It would be closed once that mission -- expected to take 20 years -- was done, the department said.
Arjun Makhijani, president of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research, criticized the MOX fuel scheme, but said there were some improvements in the overall plan.

"This is progress over where we were a month ago because she has made a commitment to immobilize at least eight tons, and a commitment to use one of the technologies I think they should be vigorously pursuing" in immobilization, he said.
Rep. Edward Markey, of Massachusetts, ranking Democrat on the House Commerce Energy and Power subcommittee, blasted the MOX plan and called for more review of it.

"This so-called conversion of nuclear swords into electric plowshares neglects to mention how dangerous, polluting and expensive its implementation will be for the American public," Markey said in a statement.
The Nuclear Energy Institute, which represent utilities, applauded the department's announcement.
